The fixed cohort contains 1,046 homes across 22 authorities; 980 latest archived reports provide 9,126 source PDF pages.

979 reports have official CIW summaries and 1 have explicitly labelled theme extracts. 66 cohort homes have no archived report.

858 homes have at least one published theme rating and 188 have none. The four theme distributions retain missing values and use the full cohort denominator.

Published tables contain 454 specific rows: 98 Priority action and 356 Area for improvement. 112 rows are Achieved; 332 have unknown status.

91 specific action rows have no topic assignment and remain included in the whole-cohort row totals; topic charts must not be treated as a complete action inventory.

All 54,952 extracted finding rows and 5,879 sections inform the evidence map. Positive and Improvement wording counts are separate overlapping search-label cohorts.

Turn evidence into better local care

Illustrative assistant learning workflow, not a CIW assessment framework. Follow a step to the relevant local control and evidence.

Resident experience → Personal planning → Staff practice → Assurance → Resident feedback

Week 1: understand and test

Read the relevant source pages with the named local lead. Ask residents what matters; sample current records and observe actual practice. Separate achieved or historical actions from present local gaps. Adapt positive practice only where suitable.

By day 30: trial and verify

Trial a small, agreed control change. Define the record, observation and resident-feedback evidence that would show success. Assign an owner and review date; track exceptions and unintended consequences.

By day 90: sustain and listen

Repeat the same checks, seek resident and staff feedback, and verify actions remain effective. Keep what improves experience, revise what does not and bring persistent gaps to local oversight.

Medicines management

Distinct reports / 980: topic mentions 915; Positive wording 512; Improvement wording 57; matching specific action rows 36; matching Priority action category 8. These sets overlap.

What to learn and test locally

Audit medicine administration records, storage, reconciliation, PRN protocols and staff competency; document exceptions and follow-up.

Local test: Sample administration records against actual staff practice with the medicines lead.
Outcome to verify: Exceptions are detected, followed up and checked; staff demonstrate the agreed local procedure.

Suggested owner: Clinical lead / medicines lead
Evidence of success: MAR audit, competency records, storage checks and documented corrective actions; triangulate with observed practice and residents’ experience.

Positive practice to adapt — selected wording

Care and support is good as planning is person-centred and responsive, families are actively involved, and safeguarding, medication and infection-prevention arrangements support people’s safety and well-being.

What to learn and test locally

Review safeguarding escalation, incident reporting and CIW notifications. Check that staff understand local procedures and that learning reaches the team.

Local test: Walk through a local escalation scenario and trace a recent incident review.
Outcome to verify: Staff explain escalation confidently and can show how incident learning changed practice.

Suggested owner: Registered manager
Evidence of success: Escalation log, training records, incident reviews and notifications; triangulate with observed practice and residents’ experience.

Personal plans & risk assessment

Distinct reports / 980: topic mentions 965; Positive wording 399; Improvement wording 88; matching specific action rows 71; matching Priority action category 9. These sets overlap.

What to learn and test locally

Sample personal plans for individual preferences, changing needs, review dates and usable risk controls. Check that staff can apply the guidance in practice.

Local test: Compare sampled plans with current preferences, changing needs and observed care.
Outcome to verify: Plans are usable and consistent with the support people actually receive.

Suggested owner: Care lead
Evidence of success: Plan reviews, resident involvement and observed practice; triangulate with observed practice and residents’ experience.

What to learn and test locally

Review staffing against actual dependency and safe recruitment checks. Examine continuity, induction and the impact of vacancies or agency use.

Local test: Compare recent rotas and induction checks with actual support needs and continuity.
Outcome to verify: The agreed staffing arrangements work in observed practice; identified gaps receive follow-up.

Training & supervision

Distinct reports / 980: topic mentions 973; Positive wording 628; Improvement wording 61; matching specific action rows 62; matching Priority action category 13. These sets overlap.

What to learn and test locally

Reconcile the training matrix with current roles and residents' needs. Sample supervision records and assess competence, rather than attendance alone.

Local test: Ask staff to demonstrate a role-relevant skill and compare supervision evidence.
Outcome to verify: Competence is demonstrated in practice rather than inferred from attendance records alone.

Suggested owner: Training lead
Evidence of success: Training matrix, competency assessment and supervision records; triangulate with observed practice and residents’ experience.

Environment & fire safety

Distinct reports / 980: topic mentions 980; Positive wording 858; Improvement wording 80; matching specific action rows 82; matching Priority action category 18. These sets overlap.

What to learn and test locally

Review fire and premises safety, servicing, accessibility and environmental risks; verify outstanding maintenance actions and person-specific evacuation arrangements.

Local test: Walk the premises and trace sampled safety or maintenance exceptions to verification.
Outcome to verify: Identified hazards receive appropriate follow-up and checks reflect actual conditions.

Suggested owner: Estates lead / manager
Evidence of success: Safety checks, servicing, maintenance log and evacuation plans; triangulate with observed practice and residents’ experience.

Positive practice to adapt — selected wording

The provider has established robust systems to minimise infection risks, maintain the premises and equipment, and monitor safety, enabling people to achieve their outcomes in a homely and welcoming environment.

Welsh language & culture

Distinct reports / 980: topic mentions 980; Positive wording 28; Improvement wording 132; matching specific action rows 1; matching Priority action category 0. These sets overlap.

What to learn and test locally

Assess the Welsh language active offer and cultural needs proactively, including how preferences are identified and acted upon; do not equate no requests with adequate provision.

Local test: Ask how language preferences are identified and observe the active offer in practice.
Outcome to verify: People can access the agreed language and cultural support, not merely a recorded preference.

Suggested owner: Registered manager
Evidence of success: Language preferences, active-offer arrangements and accessible information; triangulate with observed practice and residents’ experience.

One person felt highly motivated by the new manager in planning “a good year ahead with lots of adventures.” The promotion of Welsh language and culture is integrated through bilingual documentation.

People’s well-being requires improvement as they are living in a home which does not consistently promote their well-being. The provider must ensure people live in a safe, clean and well-maintained environment where risks are effectively controlled, and infection prevention and control standards are consistently maintained. Leadership and management require significant improvement. The Responsible Individual (RI) has not ensured effective governance, oversight or organisational arrangements to support the safe and effective operation of the service or the delivery of consistently high-quality care. Staff recruitment is not robust and there is not enough staff employed in the home.

Official CIW summary

Brookside Care Home is a care home based in Powys, providing care and nursing support to people with a range of needs. We identified improvement in most areas since the previous inspection. At the last inspection, we issued two Priority Action Notices (PANs) and five Areas for Improvement (AFIs) relating to health and safety, personal planning, dignity and respect, Responsible Individual (RI) oversight, and staffing arrangements. During this inspection, we found sufficient progress had been made to remove one PAN and three AFIs. The remaining PAN relating to health and safety has been downgraded to an AFI because improvements have reduced the level of risk to people. Whilst some residual health and safety concerns remain, we no longer consider people to be at significant or imminent risk. We found continued improvement in staff training arrangements. However, whilst training compliance has improved it remains below the standard expected. Further work is required to ensure personal plans are consistently person-centred, outcome focused and accurately reflect people's needs. Therefore, these two AFIs remain open. Overall, leaders have demonstrated commitment to improvement and the changes made since the previous inspection are having a positive impact on people’s well-being. Ratings have improved since the last inspection. We rate Well-being and Leadership and Management as Good. This reflects improved wellbeing for people and strengthened governance arrangements. We rate Care and Support and Environment as Requires Improvement because further work is needed to ensure people’s personal plans reflect their needs and they live in an environment that fully promotes their safety and well-being.

Official CIW summary

Cadoc house and flats offer residential care for adults in Cardiff. The service promotes the building of skills, education and employment opportunities for individuals with psychological, social and behavioural needs. People’s aspirations, outcomes and well-being are at the heart of this service. The service work extremely closely with people empowering them to remain in control of their lives and care. People are encouraged to express their concerns, and their rights and dignity are upheld. People can enjoy a range of events throughout the year designed around people’s needs. People told us they are regularly involved in their care planning, and this gives them control and helps them keep on track of their goals. One person described the service as “Excellent, nothing they can do to improve.” Plans are deeply personalised and consistently strength focus. People’s medication is well managed with constant consideration to promoting independence. A range of professionals are involved, and the service excels at working with other organisations with transparency. People consistently told us care and support is excellent. The service offers flexible accommodation in the form of single bedrooms and self-contained flats. This promotes the achievement of personal outcomes and ensures that people who may require more support have that option available. It is close to a range of amenities as well as the City Centre making it easier for people to stay connected with their community The environment is homely, welcoming and clean. There is an extremely well-presented garden which includes a purpose-built arts and crafts activity room. Health and safety systems are in place and regular oversight is maintained. The Responsible Individual (RI) leads a team of professional and passionate managers who provide effective oversight and are heavily involved in the service. Quality assurance documents are effective, and person focused. Care staff receive bespoke training tailored to individuals’ needs and support. Care staff are enthusiastic in their roles and strive to support people to achieve their outcomes.

Official CIW summary

Glencourt is a small care service without nursing in Caerphilly supporting people with a range of needs and abilities. At our previous inspection, we identified significant concerns relating to the quality of care and the effectiveness of oversight by the Responsible Individual (RI), resulting in the issuance of two Priority Action Notices (PANs). At this inspection, we found significant improvements across all areas of the service and acknowledge the considerable commitment, dedication and hard work demonstrated by the provider, leaders and staff in achieving these changes. Of particular note has been the comprehensive redevelopment of people's personal plans, which are now more person-centred and outcome focused. The provider has also strengthened quality assurance arrangements, resulting in improved monitoring, oversight and accountability. A newly appointed RI has introduced more meaningful systems for regulatory visits and reporting, providing greater scrutiny and improved alignment with regulatory expectations. As a result of the progress made, we are satisfied that the concerns which led to the PANs have been addressed and both have been removed. The service has achieved ratings of ‘Good’ across all four inspection themes.

People also benefit from access to secure outdoor spaces and a range of activities and community engagement opportunities. Based on our findings, we have rated Well-being as Good, Care and Support as Good, Environment as Good, and Leadership and Management as Requires Improvement. During our inspection, we found people were supported by a caring and committed staff team who knew them well and promote their well-being and independence. People and relatives spoke positively about the home, describing it as welcoming and homely. Feedback demonstrates people are listened to and are able to influence aspects of daily life, including activities and food provision. We saw positive interactions between staff and people throughout the inspection and found people are supported to access healthcare services when required. The home is generally clean, comfortable and well maintained. However, our review of care records identified that care plans, risk assessments and daily recordings do not always fully reflect people's current needs or consistently evidence the care and support provided. Whilst we did not find evidence that people are receiving unsafe care, improvements are needed to strengthen care planning and recording systems. An Area for Improvement (AFI) was identified within Care and Support. Leadership arrangements have supported improvements in several areas, including staff training and development. However, governance and quality assurance systems do not always effectively identify or address issues relating to care records, recruitment documentation and oversight of quality assurance processes. An AFI was identified within Leadership and Management, and this theme is rated as Requires Improvement.

The majority of people and relatives we spoke to gave positive feedback regarding Shillings care home. Whilst we note the provider is responsive and has tried to seek external support to aid in quality, the provider has continued to fail to drive, embed and sustain improvements from previous inspections. Governance and oversight of quality is insufficient as the systems in place have failed to identify improvements and therefore systems cannot be relied upon as being accurate and effective. This requires significant improvement.

Official CIW summary

People living at Stanley Villa experience positive outcomes and benefit from a recovery-focused service where they are treated with dignity, respect, and compassion. People spoke positively about the support they receive and the impact the service has had on their wellbeing, independence, and recovery. We observed staff and managers to have warm and professional relationships with people, and there were opportunities for individuals to contribute to decisions about the service. The environment is clean, comfortable, and generally supports people's recovery needs. However, outcomes for people require significant improvement in several areas. We identified significant concerns regarding medication management, care planning, and workforce management. Personal plans were not always complete or sufficiently detailed to guide staff in meeting people's assessed needs and managing identified risks. Medication management systems were ineffective, with concerns relating to administration, stock control, staff competence, and auditing arrangements. In addition, there were deficits in recruitment processes, staff registration, and mandatory training, reducing assurance that staff have the necessary skills and competence to provide safe care and support. As a result, we have issued Priority Action Notices. While management and oversight arrangements are in place, they are not effective in identifying and addressing these shortfalls. The provider must also strengthen governance systems, quality assurance processes, and aspects of environmental risk management to ensure people consistently receive safe, high-quality care and support.

Ongoing staffing pressures meant people did not always receive person-centred care in line with their personal plans. Governance and oversight arrangements were not consistently effective. Leaders missed opportunities to identify issues promptly and take timely action. Staff delegation, supervision and development also require strengthening to ensure staff have the skills, knowledge and support they need to meet people’s needs safely and consistently. We identified areas for improvement during this inspection and expect the provider to make improvements to achieve better outcomes for people. .

People’s well-being requires improvement because they do not always have choice and control over their daily lives or receive support that consistently promoted their rights, independence and personal outcomes. Leadership and management require significant improvement as governance, oversight and quality assurance arrangements are ineffective. The Responsible Individual (RI) has not ensured robust organisational systems are in place to support the safe and effective operation of the service. Management oversight is weak, with auditing, monitoring and quality assurance processes failing to identify a range of concerns relating to personal planning, falls oversight, medicines management, record keeping, risk management, training, staff deployment and the environment.

People are generally treated with kindness, dignity and respect and live in an environment that supports their well-being. However, inconsistencies in care documentation and monitoring records limit assurance that people’s health, personal care and social needs are always met effectively. Care and Support is rated Requires Significant Improvement. There are continued inconsistencies regarding personal planning, medication management and record keeping. Personal plans do not always provide clear, accurate or person-centred guidance. Medication errors and weaknesses in oversight processes were also found. Due to the seriousness of these issues, Priority Action Notices were re-issued. The service provides a generally safe, clean and homely environment. Living spaces support people’s comfort and safety. Communal areas offer opportunities for social interaction and relaxation. Leadership and Management is rated Requires Improvement. Although some progress has been made since previous inspections, quality assurance and governance systems have not been effective in identifying and addressing ongoing concerns. Further improvements are required to strengthen oversight, ensure compliance and secure sustained positive outcomes for people using the service. The provider has acknowledged the areas of concern identified in the inspection. They have assured us actions are underway to make the necessary improvements and provide additional leadership and management oversight. Further embedding of these actions is required to ensure the required improvements are made.

Method, attribution and limitations

  1. This is a fixed all-data period cohort, not a dashboard-filter cohort. Only each service's latest archived report is included; this is not the complete historical inspection series or a trend in care quality. Early empty periods must not be interpreted as an absence of historical inspections: earlier reports are outside this latest-only archive.
  2. Monthly membership uses reportPublishedActualDate, not the inspection visit or report issue date. Visit start/end, issue and publication are distinct. Empty months mean no latest archived report was published in that month, not that CIW did no inspections.
  3. Ratings are the exact four published directory-snapshot theme values. Their effective dates are not independently auditable and cannot be assumed to match the historical publication month. Missing ratings and missing reports are not evidence of poor care. No overall quality score is calculated.
  4. Positive wording and Improvement wording are automated search labels, not independent CIW findings. Topic counts mean reports mentioning a topic, not failures; topics and evidence sets overlap and must not be added together.
  5. Published action-table rows can be historical or Achieved. New and Reviewed describe status words published in the source, not validation today. Missing status means unknown, not unresolved. Category counts are not counts of current failures or confirmed enforcement notices.
  6. Excerpts and official summaries retain extracted wording and PDF page provenance. Layout changes and damaged characters can occur; the archived PDF is authoritative. Representative examples are not an exhaustive account or a prevalence estimate.
  7. Public latest-report URLs can change after this snapshot. Use the linked local archived PDF to verify the captured evidence; the external source link establishes its CIW origin.
  8. Management controls and the illustrative learning workflow are assistant-suggested local learning prompts, not CIW requirements, legal advice, clinical advice or an accreditation assessment. Validate applicability with appropriate local leads.
  9. CareLens Cymru is independent and not an official CIW product. The Haven has no extracted notice; the general CIW copyright page provides Crown-material reuse permission. Source links and attribution are retained.
